title: JSON Web Token (JWT)

hero.subtitle: A compact, URL-safe token format for securely transmitting claims between parties, the backbone of modern API authentication.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
JSON Web Token (JWT) is a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims to be transferred between two parties. The claims are encoded as a JSON object that is used as the payload of a JSON Web Signature (JWS) structure or as the plaintext of a JSON Web Encryption (JWE) structure.

JWTs are ubiquitous in modern web development. They're used for authentication tokens, API keys, single sign-on, and information exchange between microservices.
sections.plainLanguage: A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a compact, URL-safe way to pass claims, which are statements about a user or other entity, between two parties. The claims form a JSON object that is signed or encrypted. JWTs are widely used for authentication tokens, single sign-on and information exchange between services.

sections.title: JWT Structure
sections.content:
A signed JWT (JWS Compact Serialization) is composed of three parts separated by dots: Header, Payload, and Signature. An encrypted JWT uses five parts instead.

JWT Structure
HEADER.PAYLOAD.SIGNATURE

Base64URL(Header) + "." +
Base64URL(Payload) + "." +
Base64URL(Signature)
HeaderJSON object specifying the algorithm (alg) and token type (typ)
PayloadJSON object containing the claims (sub, iss, exp, iat, etc.)
SignatureSignature or MAC (for example HMAC or RSA) over the encoded Header and Payload
sections.plainLanguage: A signed JWT has three parts separated by dots: a header, a payload and a signature. The header names the algorithm and token type. The payload holds the claims. The signature, computed over the first two parts, lets the receiver detect changes. An encrypted JWT has five parts.

sections.title: JWT Claims
sections.content:
Claims are statements about an entity (typically the user) and additional data. There are registered, public, and private claims.

issIssuer - who created the token
subSubject - who the token is about
audAudience - intended recipient
expExpiration time (Unix timestamp)
iatIssued at time
nbfNot before time
jtiJWT ID - unique identifier for the token
sections.plainLanguage: Claims are statements about the user or token. Common ones are iss (issuer), sub (subject), aud (audience), exp (expiration time), iat (issued at), nbf (not before) and jti (unique token ID).

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Always Verify Signatures
Never trust a JWT without verifying its signature. Do not blindly trust the token's own "alg" header: check it against the algorithms your application expects.
Avoid "alg: none"
The "none" algorithm must be rejected unless explicitly expected. It has been the source of critical vulnerabilities.
Use Short Expiration
JWTs cannot be revoked once issued. Keep expiration times short and use refresh tokens for long sessions.
Don't Store Secrets in Payload
JWT payloads are only Base64URL-encoded, not encrypted. Anyone can read the claims.
sections.plainLanguage: Always verify a JWT's signature, and check its alg header against the algorithms you expect. Reject none unless it is explicitly expected. JWTs cannot be revoked once issued, so keep expiry times short. Payloads are only encoded, not encrypted, so anyone can read them.

subtitle: A compact, URL-safe token format for securely transmitting claims between parties.
summary: A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a small, URL-safe package of claims, such as who a user is and when a login expires. The claims are a JSON object that is either digitally signed or encrypted using the JOSE standards, so the receiver can check they were not tampered with. JWTs are widely used for sign-in tokens and API access.

plainLanguage.summary: A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a compact, URL-safe package of claims, such as who a user is and when a login expires. The claims are a JSON object that is signed or encrypted, so the receiver can check they were not altered. JWTs are widely used for sign-in tokens and API access.

tldr.problem: Two parties need to pass statements about a user or client in places with little room, such as an HTTP Authorization header or a URL.
tldr.mechanism: Encode the statements (claims) as a JSON object, then sign it as a JSON Web Signature or encrypt it as a JSON Web Encryption, and write the result as dot-separated Base64url text.
tldr.outcome: A self-contained token any service can verify without calling the issuer, though it is only encoded unless encrypted, and cannot be recalled once issued.

facts.label: Registered claims
facts.value: iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, jti

today: JWTs are everywhere in web authentication. They are the ID token format in OpenID Connect and a common access-token format for OAuth 2.0 APIs, and most languages have JWT libraries. Practical experience has taught the lessons the RFC hints at: libraries that trusted the token's own alg header, including none, led to forgery bugs, so current guidance (RFC 8725) tells implementations to check the algorithm against an allow-list.

data.title: A JOSE header and claims set (RFC 7519 examples)
data.code:
# JOSE header
{"typ":"JWT",
 "alg":"HS256"}

# Base64url of that header
eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLA0KICJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9

# JWT claims set (the payload)
{"iss":"joe",
 "exp":1300819380,
 "http://example.com/is_root":true}

# Unsecured JWT header (alg none) and its encoding
{"alg":"none"}
eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0
